title: The stone Buddhas
hookLine: at Gal Vihara in Polonnaruwa, great Buddhas carved from one rock, standing, seated, lying

cards: A long face of granite, in the old royal city of Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka. Out of it, sculptors cut the Buddha: seated in meditation, standing with arms folded, and lying on his side.
Nothing was carried in and set in place. The figures were uncovered, the stone around them cut away, so that each one is still part of the hill. The place is called Gal Vihara, the rock monastery.

teach.b: First, the place. The later chronicle credits King Parakramabahu with rebuilding Polonnaruwa as a royal city of parks, reservoirs and monasteries, and with the rock monastery itself.

Second, the seated Buddha. He sits in meditation, hands resting in his lap, with a calm the stone holds without effort. Behind him the rock is carved with small details, as if he sits in a shrine of his own.
Third, the standing figure, arms folded across his chest. Who is he? People disagree.
Some say the Buddha himself, in the days after his awakening.
Others say Ananda, his companion and attendant, standing in grief beside his dying teacher. The stone doesn't say, and the debate is still open. Fourth, the lying Buddha.
In the account of the Buddha's last days, the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, he lies down on his right side, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clear, between two sal trees.
The great reclining figure lies just that way, his head on a pillow. Some see a sleeping Buddha. Others see the final passing.
The chronicle doesn't say why the sculptors chose to work in a single rock. What the stone shows is simple: nothing is stacked or joined. The figures share one body with the hill.
And a stone Buddha does not fidget, does not check the time, does not shift its weight. Part of what people come for is to sit near that stillness.

how: Pilgrims at Gal Vihara remove their shoes, offer flowers and sit or stand quietly before the figures; in Buddhist temples, seated and reclining images serve as a focus for meditation and devotion.

games.q: the stone Buddhas: tap the pairs.

s: the figures were carved separately and set against the rock
they were cut from the rock itself and are still part of the hill.
people disagree about who the standing figure is
some say the Buddha himself, others Ananda grieving his teacher.
the sutta says the Buddha lay on his left side at the end
he lay on his right side, one foot resting on the other.

games.q: the Buddha is lying down for the last time between two sal trees. how does the sutta say he lies?
o: on his back, hands folded on his chest.
on his right side, one foot resting on the other.
games.why: the Mahaparinibbana Sutta says he lay on his right side, one foot on the other, mindful and clear. the reclining figure at Gal Vihara lies the same way.

practice: Find a steady seat, hands resting in your lap, back upright the way stone is upright without trying, and for a while try not to adjust.
When an itch or the urge to shift comes, see whether it can pass the way weather passes over rock; if you need to move, move gently, and settle again.

wordCard.voice: Gal Vihara. The rock monastery at Polonnaruwa where the Buddha was cut seated, standing and lying from a single face of granite. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: parinibbana, the Buddha's final passing, which the reclining figure is often read to show.

carryVoice: Your line: carved from one rock. Seated, standing and lying, all one hill. See you tomorrow.
